sources.title: How can I ensure my community tank is peaceful?
Siamese fighting fish need more space in pet shops: new behaviour data
Water temperature affects aggressive interactions in a Neotropical cichlid fish
Cá Xiêm Nuôi Chung Với Cá Nào? Gợi Ý Các Loài Cá Phù Hợp Nhất

facts.fact: Fish chosen for one tank should be able to live in the same kind of environment and be likely to get along with each other.
Fish compete with each other for food, mates and space.
Fish set up a pecking order, and it can change as they grow, so a tank that was calm can become unsettled.
Many territorial species defend one spot, such as driftwood, a cave, a rock or floating plants, mostly to protect breeding sites, eggs or fry.
Territorial fish are most aggressive toward members of their own species of the same sex.
Fish partly judge rivals by colour, pattern and shape. Bettas sometimes attack non-betta fish that are red, such as platies or serpae tetras.
Tiger barbs kept in small groups chase other fish and nip their fins.
Most aggression in community tanks comes from impulse buying rather than planned stocking.
A single angelfish, male livebearers and many barbs can become disruptive when they have no outlet for their social instincts.
Aggression problems may only start once fish reach sexual maturity.
In a tank too small for a breeding pair of cichlids such as angelfish to hold its own territory, the pair may turn aggressive toward the other fish.
Signs of fighting include split fins, a fish that suddenly hides, fish changing territories, scratches, scrapes, torn lips, missing scales, open wounds or sores, and a missing eye.
Fins split by fighting look different from the ragged edges caused by tail (fin) rot.
Healthy fish have smooth, unblemished scales, fins and skin, bright eyes and steady swimming. Circling, drifting or listlessness can point to disease.
At first, let fish settle the pecking order on their own. Splitting up fights with a net often only puts off the problem.
Put the bully in a net breeder ('fishy jail') for about a week. Move the victim out only if its injuries are severe.
A bare 5- or 10-gallon quarantine tank with a cover or glass canopy and a small filter (a sponge filter is suggested) can be used to isolate or treat a fish.
Injured fish need clean water, good food and isolation. A slime-coat conditioner can also be used.
Chewy's editors list one teaspoon of salt per gallon for injured fish, iodine or mercurochrome put on wounds, and antibiotics (kanamycin, triple sulfa or furanoids) for severe injuries.
Step 1: Before buying, look up each species' temperament and social needs. Fin-nippers and aggressive species are usually well documented.
Step 2: Make sure the aquarium is properly set up and has been running for a while before adding any fish.
Step 3: Buy only healthy fish from a clean tank where the other fish also look healthy.
Step 4: When adding new fish, rearrange the decorations so newcomers are not left without a territory.
Step 5: Watch for signs of fighting. If a fish keeps bullying others, isolate it for a while or remove it.
Rearrange the decorations so fish have to set up new territories, and add hiding places and visual barriers.
Keep shoaling fish in proper group sizes, because some species only behave normally in a group.
Chewy's editors say keeping tiger barbs in groups of at least six usually guarantees good behaviour.
Before keeping cichlid pairs such as angelfish, make sure the tank is big enough for them to defend a breeding territory.

Researchers recommend at least 5.6 litres for displaying and selling Siamese fighting fish, and larger tanks for pet bettas. Tanks should have gravel, live plants and hiding places, and be wider rather than taller.
Male bettas in small or bare tanks swam repetitively, hovered motionless for long periods and interacted more with the tank walls. Fish in larger tanks were more active.
Buying fish on impulse without checking whether they are compatible is the main mistake behind aggression in community tanks.
Keeping nippy schooling fish such as tiger barbs in too small a group makes them chase and nip their tankmates.
Separating fighting fish with a net every time often only puts off the conflict.

In Vietnam the betta is called 'cá xiêm'. Tankmates often suggested for it there are cá chuột (Corydoras), cá neon, cá tam giác (harlequin rasbora), female guppies (cá bảy màu cái), cá tỳ bà/lau kính, and snails such as ốc Nerita and small ốc táo.

Fish Vietnamese keepers are told not to keep with cá xiêm: another male betta (cá xiêm trống), male guppies (cá bảy màu đực) and other long-finned, brightly coloured fish, tiger barbs and other fin-nippers, and small fish or shrimp it could eat.

Hot season: in the cichlid Cichlasoma paranaense, raising the water 6 °C above 27 °C had no measurable effect on aggression in fish kept alone or in groups. The authors say effects of long-term high temperatures cannot be ruled out.
In the same study, lowering the temperature 6 °C below 27 °C reduced both swimming activity and aggressive interactions. The species' critical thermal maximum was 39 °C.
Male bettas differ in personality and preferences, so each fish's needs should be considered on its own.
